quizzes.title: Week 1 Language Check
quizzes.description:
Week 1 Language Check
Module 4 · Week 1
20 points10 questionsOne try
Questions 1-5 · Grammar
Common and proper nouns
 
Questions 6-10 · Words
serftreasonusurperliveryyeoman

questions.text: Which of these is a proper noun?
questions.feedback_correct: Right: Sherwood Forest names one specific place, so it is a proper noun and takes capitals.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A proper noun names one specific, particular thing by its own name. Which choice does that?

questions.text: A common noun is best described as

answers.text: a word that always takes a capital letter
a word that names any member of a group
the name of one specific person
a word that shows an action

questions.feedback_correct: Right: a common noun (sheriff, town, king) names any member of a group and stays lowercase.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A common noun names a kind of thing, not one specific named thing. The specific-name kind is a proper noun.

questions.text: In "the cruel sheriff hunted the poor folk," which word is a common noun?
questions.feedback_correct: Right: sheriff names a kind of officer here, not one named person, so it is a common noun.
questions.feedback_incorrect: "Cruel" and "poor" describe; "hunted" is an action. Which word names a kind of person?

questions.text: Which sentence capitalizes the proper noun correctly?
questions.feedback_correct: Right: the specific name Prince John is capitalized, and the plain words stay lowercase.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Capitalize the name (Prince John) and only the name. Do not lowercase the name or capitalize ordinary words.

questions.text: Which list contains only proper nouns?
questions.feedback_correct: Right: Nottingham, King Richard, and England each name one specific place or person.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Every word in the list must name one specific person or place. Some of these are general kinds of things.

questions.text: The Saxon poor are treated as mere serfs, bound to till the land for their lords. A serf is

answers.text: a poor peasant bound to work a lord's land

questions.feedback_correct: Right: a serf is a poor peasant bound to a lord's land, with almost no rights.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A serf is the lowest, bound rank of the poor: not a free farmer or an officer.

questions.text: Robin is falsely accused of treason. Treason means

answers.text: the crime of betraying your king or country

questions.feedback_correct: Right: treason is betraying your king or country; the charge against Robin is a lie.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Treason is a crime of betrayal against the king or country, not an object or a contest.

questions.text: Green calls Prince John a usurper. A usurper is

answers.text: someone who seizes power that is not rightfully theirs
a loyal servant of the king

questions.feedback_correct: Right: a usurper grabs power he has no right to; Prince John seizes the throne while Richard lives.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A usurper takes power unjustly. A loyal servant or a poor farmer is the opposite idea.

questions.text: The Sheriff's soldiers wore his livery as they closed in. Livery means

answers.text: the uniform or colors that show whose servant a man is

questions.feedback_correct: Right: livery is the colors or uniform a lord's men wear so you know whom they serve.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Livery is clothing that marks whose man a soldier is, not a weapon or a place.

questions.text: Which sentence uses yeoman correctly?

answers.text: "The king signed the yeoman into law."
"She wore a yeoman of white silk."
"The free yeoman farmed his own small plot of land."
"They sharpened the yeoman before the battle."

questions.feedback_correct: Right: a yeoman is a free man who farms his own land, ranking above a serf.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A yeoman is a person: a free small farmer: not a law, a cloth, or a weapon.

quizzes.title: Week 2 Language Check
quizzes.description:
Week 2 Language Check
Module 4 · Week 2
20 points10 questionsOne try
Questions 1-5 · Grammar
Compound sentences
 
Questions 6-10 · Words
betraytitheguilequarter-staffvaliant

questions.text: What kind of sentence is "Marian came into the room in Lincoln green."?
questions.feedback_correct: One complete thought with one subject and verb: simple.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look for a second complete thought joined on. There is only one, so it is simple.

questions.text: What kind of sentence is "Robin lost the fight, but he welcomed the winner."?
questions.feedback_correct: Two complete thoughts joined by a comma and but.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Could each half stand alone? Yes, and a comma plus a joining word connects them.

questions.text: Which fixes the run-on "The bridge was narrow neither man would give way"?

answers.text: The bridge was narrow, neither man would give way.
The bridge was narrow, and neither man would give way.
The bridge was narrow and, neither man would give way.
The bridge, was narrow neither man would give way.

questions.feedback_correct: A comma plus and joins the two thoughts.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A fix needs a comma and a joining word, placed between the two thoughts.

questions.text: Which is a correctly punctuated compound sentence?

answers.text: Much hid in a hollow tree, and the horsemen did not find him.
Much hid in a hollow tree, the horsemen did not find him.
Much hid in a hollow tree and, the horsemen did not find him.
Much hid in a hollow tree the horsemen did not find him.

questions.feedback_correct: Comma, then and, between two complete thoughts.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look for the choice with both a comma and a joining word, in the right place.

questions.text: Which sentence is a run-on?

answers.text: Robin blew his horn, and Will Scarlet came running.
Robin blew his horn Will Scarlet came running.
Will Scarlet and many men came out of the thicket.

questions.feedback_correct: Two complete thoughts run together with no comma or joining word.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A run-on pushes two complete thoughts together. Which choice has no comma and no joining word between them?

questions.text: Will Scarlet says he is no villain "who would betray a good and generous master for any bribe." To betray someone is to

answers.text: pay someone back for a kindness
be disloyal to someone who trusts you
hide from someone who is searching

questions.feedback_correct: To betray is to be disloyal to someone who trusts you.
questions.feedback_incorrect: He says he would not do it for a bribe. Think of a servant who sells out his master.

questions.text: The old groom says the new masters will take a tithe of their savings as a fine. A tithe is

answers.text: a gift given to the poor
a written order from the king
a tenth part taken as a payment
a fee for crossing a bridge

questions.feedback_correct: A tithe is a tenth part taken as a payment or fine.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The groom calls it a fine, and tithe is about a tenth. It is taken from them, not given.

questions.text: Robin says, "force cannot save him, but guile may." Guile means
questions.feedback_correct: Guile is clever trickery, the opposite of force.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Robin sets guile against force. It is what you use when strength will not work.

questions.text: Robin cuts "a quarter-staff such as your own" to fight the stranger on the bridge. A quarter-staff is

answers.text: a long, stout wooden pole held in both hands
a short sword worn at the belt

questions.feedback_correct: A quarter-staff is a long, stout wooden pole held in both hands.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Robin cuts it from the thicket and the two men fight with it on the bridge. It is a pole, not a blade or a bow.

questions.text: The poem that opens Chapter 3 says, "An hundred valiant men had this brave Robin Hood." Valiant means
questions.feedback_correct: Valiant means brave and determined.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The poem praises his hundred men next to the word brave. Which choice is praise for fighting men?

quizzes.title: Week 3 Language Check
quizzes.description:
Week 3 Language Check
Module 4 · Week 3
20 points10 questionsOne try
Questions 1-5 · Grammar
Subject-verb agreement
 
Questions 6-10 · Words
prosperousabbotsuretyhermitalms

questions.text: Choose the verb: "Sir Richard of Legh ___ four hundred pounds to the Abbot of St Mary's."
questions.feedback_correct: One person, present tense: owes.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Match the verb to the subject. Sir Richard is one person, so the verb is singular.

questions.text: Choose the verb: "The Abbot of St Mary's ___ rents from his tenants in his abbey."
questions.feedback_correct: Abbot is one person, so the verb is receives.
questions.feedback_incorrect: One person, present tense: pick the singular verb.

questions.text: Which word is the true subject? "A band of foresters in Lincoln green comes to the archery contest."
questions.feedback_correct: Band is the subject. Of foresters only describes it, and comes is singular.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Cross out of foresters and in Lincoln green. The verb is comes. What one thing comes?

questions.text: Choose the verb: "Marian and the Friar ___ at the bridge at Gamwell."
questions.feedback_correct: Two people joined by and take a plural verb: stand.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Count the people. Marian and the Friar is two, so the verb is plural.

questions.text: Which sentence has correct agreement?

answers.text: The hermit of Copmanhurst carry travelers across the ford.
Robin and Little John waits in the camp.
Friar Tuck and Robin shares a venison pasty in the hermitage.
Friar Tuck and Robin share a venison pasty in the hermitage.

questions.feedback_correct: Friar Tuck and Robin is two people, so share agrees.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Check each subject. One person takes a singular verb. Two people joined by and take a plural verb.

questions.text: Sir Richard sighs that he was once "rich and prosperous." Prosperous means

answers.text: doing well, with plenty of money and success

questions.feedback_correct: Prosperous means doing well, with plenty of money and success.
questions.feedback_incorrect: He says he was prosperous, but now he has lost nearly everything. The word names the good fortune he lost.

questions.text: The Abbot of St Mary's holds Sir Richard's debt. An abbot is

answers.text: the head of a village market
a knight who serves a king
a forester who guards a forest

questions.feedback_correct: An abbot is the head of a monastery.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The Abbot sits in his abbey with his monks about him. Who leads a monastery?

questions.text: Sir Richard has only his word as surety. A surety is

answers.text: a pledge that guarantees a promise or a loan

questions.feedback_correct: A surety is a pledge that guarantees a loan. Sir Richard can offer only his word.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The Abbot lent the money on a surety. Think of what stands behind a loan.

questions.text: Friar Tuck calls himself "the plain Hermit of Copmanhurst." A hermit is

answers.text: a person who lives alone, often for religious reasons

questions.feedback_correct: A hermit lives alone, often for religious reasons.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Friar Tuck lives by himself at the ford. Look for the choice about living alone.

questions.text: "I do but ask for alms," says the Friar. Alms are

answers.text: a fee owed to the king
money or gifts given to the poor

questions.feedback_correct: Alms are money or gifts given to the poor.
questions.feedback_incorrect: He is asking at the ford, and alms are what is given to people in need.

quizzes.title: Week 4 Language Check
quizzes.description:
Week 4 Language Check
Module 4 · Week 4
20 points10 questionsOne try
Questions 1-5 · Grammar
Verb tense
 
Questions 6-10 · Words
proclaimquiverdisguisetollambush

questions.text: Which sentence has an unnecessary tense shift?

answers.text: Robin wins the silver arrow and kneels before Prince John.
Robin won the silver arrow and knelt before Prince John.
Robin wins the silver arrow and knelt before Prince John.
Robin will win the silver arrow and will kneel before Prince John.

questions.feedback_correct: Wins is present and knelt is past, with no change in time to explain it.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Find the sentence that mixes present and past for no reason. The others keep one tense throughout.

questions.text: Keep the tense steady: "In Chapter 9, Sir Richard arrives late and ___ Robin a hundred yew bows."
questions.feedback_correct: Arrives is present, so brings keeps the tense steady.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Arrives is present. The next verb should match it.

questions.text: Which sentence changes tense for a good reason?

answers.text: Sir Richard borrowed four hundred pounds last year, and today he brings it back.
Little John searches the saddle-bags and found eight hundred pounds.
The Sheriff follows the Butcher and rode deeper into Sherwood.
Sir Guy whispers to Prince John and left the stand.

questions.feedback_correct: The time really changes, from last year to today.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A tense change is fine only when the time changes. Look for time words like last year and today.

questions.text: Which sentence is consistent in tense?

answers.text: The Sheriff followed the Butcher into the forest and hears the horn.
The Sheriff follows the Butcher into the forest and hears the horn.
The Sheriff will follow the Butcher into the forest and heard the horn.
The Sheriff follows the Butcher into the forest and heard the horn.

questions.feedback_correct: Follows and hears are both present.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Find the choice where both verbs are in the same tense.

questions.text: A classmate writes: "Prince John gives Robin the arrow, and Robin thanked him." The best fix is
questions.feedback_correct: Gives is present, so thanks keeps the sentence steady.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The two verbs do not match. Fix the verb, not the name or the time.

questions.text: Prince John had proclaimed a great archery meeting. To proclaim is to
questions.feedback_correct: To proclaim is to announce officially and publicly.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The prince tells everyone about the meeting. Think of a public announcement.

questions.text: Robin wants to drop the silver arrow into his quiver. A quiver is
questions.feedback_correct: A quiver is a case for carrying arrows.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Robin drops an arrow into it. Think of what an archer carries arrows in.

questions.text: Robin says he can go to the contest in disguise. A disguise is

answers.text: a change of appearance that hides who you are

questions.feedback_correct: A disguise changes your appearance to hide who you really are.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Robin is an outlaw who still wants to enter the contest. What would let him do that unseen?

questions.text: Robin stops the butcher on the road and says he "has never paid any toll to us." A toll is

answers.text: a bell rung at a fair
a payment charged for passing along a road

questions.feedback_correct: A toll is a payment charged for passing along a road or over a bridge.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Robin says the butcher has never paid it, on a road Robin's band watches. Think of a charge for passing.

questions.text: Sir Guy's men take Sir Richard captive from an ambush while he is out hawking. An ambush is

answers.text: a surprise from a hiding place

questions.feedback_correct: An ambush is a surprise from a hiding place.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The men fell upon him while he was out hawking. What kind of attack comes from hiding?

quizzes.title: Week 5 Language Check
quizzes.description:
Week 5 Language Check
Module 4 · Week 5
20 points10 questionsOne try
Questions 1-5 · Grammar
Complex sentences
 
Questions 6-10 · Words
pretencetannerminstrelpresumptionguardian

questions.text: Which group of words is a dependent clause?
questions.feedback_correct: When the bridegroom came has a subject and a verb but cannot stand alone.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A dependent clause cannot stand as a sentence. Which group leaves you waiting for more?

questions.text: Which sentence is a complex sentence?

answers.text: Robin laughed, and he chased the beggar.
Robin chased the beggar because the beggar had taken John's clothes.

questions.feedback_correct: One complete thought plus a part that starts with because.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A complex sentence has one complete thought and one dependent clause. Look for a word like because.

questions.text: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?

answers.text: When Robin reached the church everyone was, waiting for the bride.
When Robin reached, the church everyone was waiting for the bride.
When Robin reached the church, everyone was waiting for the bride.
When Robin reached the church everyone, was waiting for the bride.

questions.feedback_correct: A comma follows the opening When clause.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The comma goes after the whole opening clause, right before the main thought.

questions.text: Which starter word makes the sentence true to Chapter 13? "___ Arthur-a-Bland had sworn to be loyal, Robin led him to the secret glade to eat and drink."
questions.feedback_correct: Arthur swore first, then Robin led him to eat. After gives the true order.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Ask what happened first in the chapter, and pick the word that keeps that order.

questions.text: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?

answers.text: Arthur, paid the innkeeper because he owed ten shillings.
Arthur paid the innkeeper because he owed ten shillings.
Arthur paid, the innkeeper because he owed ten shillings.
Arthur paid the innkeeper because, he owed ten shillings.

questions.feedback_correct: The dependent clause comes last, so no comma is needed.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A comma does not belong between a subject and its verb, or inside the clause. Here the main thought comes first.

questions.text: Robin had untied the three prisoners' bonds "while making pretence to secure them." Pretence means

answers.text: a false show meant to make others believe something untrue

questions.feedback_correct: A pretence is a false show meant to make others believe something untrue.
questions.feedback_incorrect: He unties the ropes while looking as if he ties them tighter. Think of a false show.

questions.text: Arthur-a-Bland bought skins and sold them cured and dressed. A tanner is a person who
questions.feedback_correct: A tanner turns animal skins into leather.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Arthur's work is with skins, cured and dressed. Who turns skins into leather?

questions.text: Allin-a-Dale carried a small harp and sang. A minstrel is
questions.feedback_correct: A minstrel is a traveling singer and musician.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Allin-a-Dale carries a harp and sings. Which choice fits a harp and a song?

questions.text: The beggar says he punished Little John "for his presumption." Presumption means

answers.text: boldness that goes past what is proper

questions.feedback_correct: Presumption is boldness that goes past what is proper.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The beggar says he punished Little John for it. Think of a fault, not a feeling.

questions.text: The Bishop says he is the bride's "legal guardian" because her parents are dead. A guardian is

answers.text: a person who sings at weddings
a person legally responsible for looking after someone
a person who owns a castle

questions.feedback_correct: A guardian is a person legally responsible for looking after someone.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Her parents are dead, so the Bishop claims the right to speak for her. Look for the choice about looking after someone.

quizzes.title: Week 6 Language Check
quizzes.description:
Week 6 Language Check
Module 4 · Week 6
20 points10 questionsOne try
Questions 1-5 · Grammar
Appositives
 
Questions 6-10 · Words
traitorseneschalvalourgenerositysworn

questions.text: An appositive is a noun phrase that

answers.text: renames the noun right next to it

questions.feedback_correct: An appositive renames the noun right next to it.
questions.feedback_incorrect: It does not show action, join sentences or ask. It renames.

questions.text: In "Blondel, Richard's faithful minstrel friend, sought him all over Europe," which part is the appositive?
questions.feedback_correct: Richard's faithful minstrel friend renames Blondel.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Find the phrase that renames Blondel, not the one that tells what he did.

questions.text: Which sentence sets off the middle appositive correctly?

answers.text: Bettris the daughter of a wealthy Justice, won George's heart.
Bettris, the daughter of a wealthy Justice, won George's heart.
Bettris, the daughter of a wealthy Justice won George's heart.
Bettris the daughter, of a wealthy Justice won George's heart.

questions.feedback_correct: A middle appositive takes a comma before it and a comma after it.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The renaming phrase needs a comma on both sides, around the whole phrase.

questions.text: Which sentence punctuates an appositive at the end correctly?

answers.text: Robin agreed, with Bettris George's bride.
Robin agreed with, Bettris George's bride.
Robin agreed with Bettris George's bride.
Robin agreed with Bettris, George's bride.

questions.feedback_correct: At the end, the appositive follows a comma and renames Bettris.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Put one comma right after the noun the phrase renames.

questions.text: In "Sir Guy of Gisborne, Robin's sworn enemy, rode past with a dozen men," the appositive renames
questions.feedback_correct: Robin's sworn enemy renames Sir Guy of Gisborne.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Ask who is Robin's sworn enemy. The appositive renames that person.

questions.text: Robin says Worman served him "until it served your turn better to betray me." A person who betrays a trust is a
questions.feedback_correct: A traitor is a person who betrays a trust or a side.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Robin names the betrayal in his own words. Which choice names the person who betrays?

questions.text: The Sheriff lends the Bishop "my seneschal Worman," who was once Robin's steward. A seneschal is

answers.text: the chief household officer of a lord

questions.feedback_correct: A seneschal is the chief household officer of a lord, a steward.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The text calls Worman Robin's former steward. A seneschal does a steward's work.

questions.text: A ballad praises "The pinner's valour, and how firm he stood." Valour means

answers.text: great courage in the face of danger

questions.feedback_correct: Valour is great courage in the face of danger.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The ballad praises how firm he stood. Think of courage, not temper or boasting.

questions.text: When the two priests' pockets turn out to hold over six hundred gold pieces, Friar Tuck teases them: "Heaven has taught you generosity." Generosity is

answers.text: a habit of telling the truth
a willingness to give freely to others

questions.feedback_correct: Generosity is a willingness to give freely to others.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Tuck jokes that the priests are now giving their money away. Which choice is about giving?

questions.text: Robin calls Sir Guy of Gisborne his "sworn enemy." Sworn here means

answers.text: bound by a vow to remain an enemy

questions.feedback_correct: Sworn here means bound by a vow to remain an enemy.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Think of someone who has sworn an oath. What is the oath here?

quizzes.title: Week 7 Language Check
quizzes.description:
Week 7 Language Check
Module 4 · Week 7
20 points10 questionsOne try
Questions 1-5 · Grammar
Quoting and citing
 
Questions 6-10 · Words
verdereroppressvengeancepardonwaylay

questions.text: Robin tells the palmer, "We dwell here to set right the wrong." Which sentence quotes him correctly?

answers.text: "We dwell here to set right the wrong" (Ch. 21) is what Robin says.
Robin tells the palmer, "We dwell here to set right the wrong" (Ch. 21).
Robin tells the palmer, we dwell here to set right the wrong (Ch. 21).
Robin tells the palmer "We dwell here to set right the wrong. (Ch. 21)"

questions.feedback_correct: Signal phrase with a comma, exact words in quotation marks, the chapter in parentheses, the period last.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Check four parts in order: signal phrase and comma, quotation marks around the exact words, chapter in parentheses, period last.

questions.text: The Black Knight tells Robin, "But be sure I will seek you out ere long." Which sentence quotes part of it correctly?

answers.text: The Black Knight promises that he will "seek you out ere long." (Ch. 20)
The Black Knight promises that he will "seek you out ere long" (Ch. 20).
The Black Knight promises that he will "seek you out ere long (Ch. 20)."
The Black Knight promises that he will "seek you out ere long" Ch. 20.

questions.feedback_correct: The chapter sits in parentheses after the closing quotation mark, and the period comes last.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Check where the chapter and the period fall around the closing quotation mark.

questions.text: Which sentence is a "dropped quote," with no signal phrase?

answers.text: "I freely pardon you, and all here present" (Ch. 21).
Richard tells Robin, "I freely pardon you" (Ch. 21).
Green writes that Richard pardons "all here present" (Ch. 21).
As the king says, "I freely pardon you" (Ch. 21).

questions.feedback_correct: It stands alone, with no signal phrase to say who is speaking.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A dropped quote has no words introducing it. Which choice just starts with the quotation?

questions.text: A writer quotes the palmer saying he is on "the King's business." Where does the chapter go?

answers.text: In parentheses after the closing quotation mark, before the sentence's period.
In parentheses at the start of the sentence.
After the period, on a new line.

questions.feedback_correct: The chapter goes in parentheses after the closing quotation mark, then the period.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The citation follows the closing quotation mark, and the sentence's period comes last.

questions.text: Green describes the palmer sitting "on his horse as still as a statue." Which sentence uses those exact words correctly?

answers.text: The palmer sat on his horse. "As still as a statue" (Ch. 21).
The palmer sat on his horse as still as a statue (Ch. 21).
Green describes the palmer sitting "on his horse as still as a statue" (Ch. 21).
The palmer "sat on his horse as still as a statue." (Ch. 21)

questions.feedback_correct: A signal phrase, the exact words in quotation marks, then the chapter and the period.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Exact words need quotation marks. Check the signal phrase, and that the chapter comes before the final period.

questions.text: Two or three verderers ride with the Sheriff's men. A verderer is

answers.text: an officer who enforced the royal Forest Laws
a pilgrim home from the Holy Land
a servant who runs a lord's house

questions.feedback_correct: A verderer is an officer who enforced the royal Forest Laws.
questions.feedback_incorrect: They ride with the Sheriff's men, so they work for the law. Think of a forest officer.

questions.text: Robin says the band harms only those who "robbed innocent men or oppressed them." To oppress people is to

answers.text: treat them cruelly and unfairly by using power over them
pay them fairly for their work
guard them from danger on the road

questions.feedback_correct: To oppress is to treat people cruelly and unfairly by using power over them.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Robin puts it beside robbing innocent men. Look for the choice that harms people.

questions.text: Prince John says he has sworn "a certain vengeance" on Robin. Vengeance means

answers.text: harm done in return for a wrong

questions.feedback_correct: Vengeance is harm done in return for a wrong.
questions.feedback_incorrect: John says it will fall heavily on a man who crossed him. Which choice pays back a wrong?

questions.text: King Richard gives Robin a pardon. A pardon is

answers.text: a seat at the king's table
a punishment ordered by a king
official forgiveness that cancels a punishment

questions.feedback_correct: A pardon is official forgiveness that cancels a punishment.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Richard says he freely pardons Robin, who has been an outlaw. What would a king give that cancels it?

questions.text: The Baron Fitzurse is sent to waylay the Black Knight in Sherwood. To waylay someone is to

answers.text: lie in wait for him and stop him on the road

questions.feedback_correct: To waylay is to lie in wait for someone and stop him on the road.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Fitzurse is sent after the Black Knight by John, who suspects who he is. Think of lying in wait.

quizzes.title: Week 8 Language Check
quizzes.description:
Week 8 Language Check
Module 4 · Week 8
20 points10 questionsOne try
Questions 1-5 · Grammar
Combining sentences
 
Questions 6-10 · Words
sanctuarymercenaryveilboonheir

questions.text: Which is the best way to combine these sentences? "Robin trusts his pardon. Robin goes to Mass in Nottingham. Robin goes alone."

answers.text: Robin trusts his pardon, Robin goes alone, Robin goes to Mass.
Trusting his pardon, Robin goes alone to Mass in Nottingham.
Robin trusts. His pardon. Alone to Mass.
Robin trusts his pardon and Robin goes alone and Robin goes to Mass.

questions.feedback_correct: One smooth sentence that keeps all three ideas.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Look for the version that joins the ideas without comma splices, fragments or a long and chain.

questions.text: Which sentence has the best varied opening?

answers.text: Little John answers the silver bugle.
Little John hears it and Little John answers.
Hearing the silver bugle, Little John answers from nearby.

questions.feedback_correct: It opens with a phrase instead of the subject.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A varied opening starts with something other than the subject, such as a phrase.

questions.text: Which sentence combines these correctly? "Robin rides on alone. He wants to lead John's men away from Marian."

answers.text: Robin rides on alone, he wants to lead John's men away from Marian.
Robin rides on alone because. He wants to lead John's men away from Marian.
Robin rides on alone because he wants to lead John's men away from Marian.
Robin rides on alone he wants to lead John's men away from Marian.

questions.feedback_correct: Because joins the reason to the main thought.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Two sentences need a joining word and the right punctuation. A bare comma or no join breaks the sentence.

questions.text: Which change is revision, not just editing?

answers.text: Moving a strong quotation to the start of a paragraph and adding a sentence that explains it.

questions.feedback_correct: Revision changes what the writing says or how it is arranged.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Fixing a comma, a spelling or a font is editing. Revision improves the ideas and their order.

questions.text: Kirkleys Nunnery opened ___ doors to Marian, and the Prioress led her to sanctuary. Which word fits?
questions.feedback_correct: Its shows that the doors belong to the nunnery.
questions.feedback_incorrect: It's means it is. The word that shows ownership has no apostrophe.

questions.text: Marian is led to sanctuary at Kirkleys. Sanctuary means

answers.text: safety given to someone in a holy place

questions.feedback_correct: Sanctuary is safety given to someone in a holy place.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Marian is sent to the Prioress, a holy woman, to be safe. Look for the choice about safety.

questions.text: King John says his men are "all mercenaries, hired abroad." A mercenary is

answers.text: a soldier who serves his own lord for free
a soldier hired for pay, often from another country

questions.feedback_correct: A mercenary is a soldier hired for pay, often from another country.
questions.feedback_incorrect: John says the men are hired abroad. Which choice is a soldier paid to fight?

questions.text: The Prioress tells Marian she can be safe if she will "take the veil." To take the veil means
questions.feedback_correct: To take the veil is to become a nun.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The Prioress says Marian must vow herself to God and join the sisterhood. What does taking the veil mean?

questions.text: Little John says, "Grant me one last boon!" A boon is

answers.text: a favour that is asked for

questions.feedback_correct: A boon is a favour that is asked for.
questions.feedback_incorrect: He says grant me a boon. Think of what a person asks for.

questions.text: The Prioress knows that Marian is "the heir to all the Locksley estates." An heir is

answers.text: a person who will receive someone's property or title when that person dies
a servant who looks after a lord's lands
a nun who leads a nunnery
a person who buys land from the king

questions.feedback_correct: An heir will receive someone's property or title when that person dies.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The text says Robin is dead and Marian would receive the estates. Who receives them?
